strengths: The SciEvents dataset addresses a genuine gap: document-level, multi-event annotation for scientific abstracts with a hierarchical schema (sub-events) and complex nugget structures (inconsecutive, overlapped, reverse-ordered), which prior event datasets (ACE2005, RAMS, WIKIEVENTS) do not cover.

The annotation process is described in unusual detail (3-stage pipeline with screening, weekly review, quality inspection, and even remuneration/time-per-document statistics), and the paper commits to releasing both the dataset and code on GitHub.

The dataset analysis (Table 1, Tables 2-4, event/argument type distributions) is quantitative and supports the central claim that scientific abstracts are denser and structurally more complex than general-domain EE data.

The proposed EC (event correlation) metric is a reasonable complement to standard TI/TC/AI/AC criteria for evaluating hierarchical event extraction, and the appendix provides a worked example of the metric computation.
The word-word grid formulation is a sensible fit for the stated problems (overlap, discontinuity, ordering), and the ablation study isolates the contributions of the biaffine and biattention modules.
weaknesses: The claim that SciEvents is 'the first scientific event extraction dataset' is overstated; prior scientific IE resources (e.g., SciIE, ScienceIE, Dr. Inventor corpus) annotate science-specific structures and should be discussed and differentiated rather than ignored.

The method is largely an adaptation of word-word relation classification (W2NER, Li et al. 2022, cited as [12]) plus biaffine parsing and CLN; the architectural novelty is modest and the paper does not clearly articulate what is new beyond extending HTL to the full grid.

Baseline comparison has fairness concerns: OneIE is trained with additional entity annotation (footnote 2), and BartGen/PAIE/UIE are paired with a separate word-word-relation ED module at inference, making them pipeline systems while EXCEEDS is end-to-end; the magnitude of EXCEEDS's advantage may partly reflect this asymmetry. No significance testing or variance reporting is provided despite averaging over runs.

No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) are reported anywhere, which is a significant omission for a dataset-contribution paper; the quality-inspection procedure is described but not quantified.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in reported numbers: Section 6.3 claims 'the highest EC F1 scores of 15.79 for Inconsecutive Nugget' while Table 4 reports only TC/AC (25.34/17.51) for that category; the dataset name alternates between SciEvents and 'SciEvent'; and the abstract/conclusion overstate claims relative to the evidence.

The domain scope is narrow: all documents come from ACL main-conference papers (2019-2022) in NLP, yet the paper repeatedly claims coverage of the 'scientific domain' broadly; generalization to other scientific fields is asserted, not shown.

Only four baselines are evaluated, all pre-LLM, despite the related-work section emphasizing LLM-based EE; given the paper's own framing, an LLM or instruction-tuned baseline (e.g., GoLLIE, InstructUIE) is a notable omission.

Method details are under-specified for reproducibility: the BiAttention equations use undefined Q_h, K_h, V_h projections, the combining of R and Z (S = R + Z) then softmax is not clearly justified dimensionally, and the three heuristic decoding rules are only sketched.

The EC evaluation example and metric definition (Appendix B.3) are hard to parse, and no error analysis beyond the four scenario splits is provided; the ablation table shows small deltas (0.34 for biattention) with no significance assessment.

strengths: The SciEvents dataset addresses a real gap: document-level, multi-event annotation of scientific abstracts with hierarchical (sub-event) structure and non-flat (inconsecutive, overlapped, reverse-ordered) nuggets is genuinely under-explored, and a released resource of this kind could be useful to the community.

The dataset construction process is documented in reasonable detail, including a multi-stage annotation pipeline with pre-annotation screening, training of directors/annotators, quality inspection loops, and disclosure of annotation time and remuneration.

The paper introduces a new evaluation criterion (Event Correlation, EC) for hierarchical events and explains the metric definitions with worked examples in the appendix, which improves the clarity of the task definition.

The grid-based formulation (building on W2NER-style word-word relation classification) is a reasonable fit for dense, overlapping nuggets, and the end-to-end design avoids pipelined ED/EAE error propagation.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Section 6.2 reports an EC F1 of 51.25 while Table 3 reports 47.60 for EXCEEDS; Section 6.3 cites an 'EC F1 of 15.79 for Inconsecutive Nugget' although Table 4 contains no EC column for that scenario and reports TC/AC values instead; the text also claims a 'Consecutive Nugget' scenario was evaluated but no such column appears in Table 4. These discrepancies suggest the empirical results were not carefully verified.

The claim that SciEvents is 'the first scientific event extraction dataset' is overstated: prior scientific IE resources (e.g., SciIE, ScienceIE, and event-like annotation in scientific NLP) are neither cited nor discussed, and the dataset covers only ACL 2019-2022 abstracts, which is NLP-specific rather than representative of the 'scientific domain' broadly.

No inter-annotator agreement scores are reported anywhere, which is a fundamental soundness requirement for an annotation-heavy resource paper; the quality-control heuristic ('over 2 conflicts returned for revision') is not a substitute for IAA statistics.

The baseline comparison has fairness and coverage problems: OneIE uses additional entity annotation and global features during training (per footnote 2) while other models do not; despite the related-work section emphasizing LLMs and zero-shot IE as recent advances, no LLM-based baseline (e.g., ChatGPT/InstructUIE-style, which the paper itself cites) is evaluated.

The method is an assembly of existing components (W2NER grid from Li et al. [12], CLN from [18], biaffine from [56], BiAttention), and the ablation results are weak evidence of the claimed design benefits: removing BiAttention causes only a 0.34 F1 drop, leaving the architectural contribution under-supported.

The evaluation protocol is asymmetric: baselines are marked '-' as 'cannot be tested' for inconsecutive and reverse-ordered nuggets, yet EXCEEDS receives scores in these cells, making the comparative claims in Table 4 hard to interpret without an explanation of why baselines could not be adapted.

Novelty is limited on the modeling side, and the 'state-of-the-art' claim holds only on the authors' own newly introduced dataset rather than established benchmarks, so the empirical contribution's general significance is unclear.

Several technical details are underspecified for reproducibility: the loss notation (cross-entropy applied to softmax outputs s_ij) is imprecise, decoding heuristics are described only informally, no code link or concrete repository is provided despite the release claim, and hyperparameter search ranges are not given.

Writing quality is below bar: terminology fluctuates (SciEvents vs. SciEvent), statistical claims in the text do not always match the tables, and Section 6.3's description of evaluated scenarios contradicts Table 4's structure.

strengths: SciEvents fills a genuine resource gap: a document-level, multi-event scientific-domain dataset with a hierarchical event schema (sub-events) and complex nugget types (inconsecutive, overlapped, reverse-ordered), which is a useful contribution for the community and enables new research directions in scientific IE.

The dataset construction process is described in detail (schema design with domain experts, multi-stage annotation pipeline with pre-annotation, screening, quality inspection), and the complete schema is provided in the appendix.
The paper introduces an additional evaluation criterion (Event Correlation, EC) tailored to hierarchical sub-events, a sensible extension of standard EE metrics.

The word-word event grid formulation (extending W2NER-style relation classification with EAL edges for trigger-argument and trigger-trigger links) is a coherent end-to-end design that can in principle handle overlapping and non-flat nuggets, and the empirical results on the new dataset show consistent advantages over the compared baselines, especially on the EC metric.
Analysis of density/complexity statistics relative to ACE2005, RAMS, WIKIEVENTS, and DICE is informative and motivates the resource.
The authors state that both the dataset and code will be released on GitHub, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: the text in Sec. 6.2 reports EC F1 of 51.25 while Table 3 reports 47.60 for EXCEEDS; Sec. 6.3 claims 'the highest EC F1 scores of 15.79 for Inconsecutive Nugget' but Table 4 contains no EC column for the Inconsecutive scenario (values are 25.34/17.51 for TC/AC). The scenario description mentions a 'Consecutive Nugget' scenario that does not appear in Table 4. These inconsistencies must be resolved.

The claim that SciEvents is 'the first scientific event extraction dataset' is overstated; prior work on scientific discourse and event extraction (e.g., SciERC-adjacent resources, scientific discourse segmentation and event/tagging schemes) exists and should be positioned against. Related scientific IE datasets are cited only sparsely.

No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) are reported despite a multi-annotator pipeline; quality control is described narratively but evidence of annotation quality is anecdotal. This is a significant gap for a dataset paper.

Baseline comparison is not fully fair and incomplete: OneIE is trained with additional entity annotation (footnote 2) unavailable to other models; generative baselines rely on a separate W2NER event-detection module; and, given the paper's own related-work discussion emphasizing LLMs, no LLM or instruction-tuned baseline is evaluated, despite such models being the current standard for assessing new EE datasets.

Methodological novelty is modest: the framework substantially reuses established components (word-word relation classification, biaffine tagging, conditional layer normalization, biattention) combined in a grid. The framing as a 'novel' method overstates the contribution; the novelty is mainly in the labeling scheme and adaptation to a new dataset.

The evaluation is limited to a single encoder (BERT, hidden size 1024) with no experiments varying encoders, and no significance testing; ablation effects are small (e.g., BiAttention removal costs only 0.34 AC F1), weakening claims about the necessity of specific components.

Dataset scope is narrower than claimed: only ACL 2019-2022 abstracts are annotated, so calling the resource representative of the 'scientific domain' at large is an overreach; generalization to other scientific fields is untested.

Missing methodological details hurt reproducibility: how grid cells are mapped to spans under overlapping structures, how trigger type interacts with grid labels, decoding hyperparameters, and the exact metric computation for EC (Appendix B.3 gives an example but not a formal definition). Additionally, inconsistencies exist in naming (SciEvents vs. SciEvent) and there are multiple typographical/grammatical errors.

Ethics/labor considerations are unaddressed: annotation was outsourced at approximately $4.5 per document (~19 minutes of work) with no ethics statement, wage fairness discussion, or annotator expertise background; an ACL-appropriate ethics statement and data statement are absent.
Error analysis is limited to scenario-level F1 breakdowns; no qualitative analysis of failure cases, and the reasons for the sharp AI/AC drop across all models are not investigated.

strengths: SciEvents is a substantial new resource: 2,508 document-level annotated scientific abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, explicitly covering complex structures (overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order nuggets, sub-events) that most existing EE datasets lack.

The dataset construction is transparent and thorough: iterative schema design with domain experts, a detailed multi-stage annotation protocol (Appendix I), quality inspection with an inspector-annotator separation policy, distribution statistics across splits (Tables 23-25, Figure 11), and fair annotator remuneration details.
The density/complexity analysis (Table 2) provides quantitative motivation by comparing SciEvents against nine established EE datasets on token-normalized density and complex-form proportions.

Evaluation is broad: ten baselines spanning global, discriminative, and generative paradigms (including an LLM-based model), a new event correlation (EC) metric for hierarchical sub-event extraction, ablations of both contextual encoding and grid refinement, error analysis (identification vs. classification errors), computational cost and complexity analysis, and a worked example of metric computation (Appendix B).

The proposed EXCEEDS framework is well-motivated: the word-word grid with HTL/THL/EAL relations offers a unified, principled way to encode hierarchical events, discontinuous arguments, and long-distance trigger-argument links in one end-to-end model, with a clearly specified decoding algorithm (Appendix A).
Reproducibility is well supported: full hyperparameters, hardware, GPU-hour costs, decoding heuristics, and stated plans to release both dataset and code.
weaknesses: The headline 'state-of-the-art' claims rest on small margins: EXCEEDS beats the strongest baseline by 0.51 (AC) and 0.53 (EC) F1, which is comparable to or only slightly above the reported standard deviations, and no statistical significance testing is provided. The TI result (75.29) does not exceed OneIE (75.72).

No inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) is reported anywhere, which is a notable gap for a resource paper whose central contribution is annotation quality; only a first-pass acceptance rate (73.05%) is given.

The dataset's domain scope is narrow relative to the 'scientific domain' framing: only ACL conference abstracts (NLP sub-domain, 2019-2022), acknowledged in the Limitations section, which weakens generalizability claims of both the benchmark and conclusions about scientific EE broadly.

The grid-based formulation is architecturally close to existing token-pair relation methods (UIE-style semantic matching, global pointer approaches); the technical novelty of EXCEEDS itself is moderate, and the O(l²) grid memory restricts applicability to longer documents, which the paper sidesteps by using only abstracts.

Performance on the complex forms that most motivate the paper remains weak with high variance (e.g., reverse-order nugget F1 of 7.27±5.14 for EXCEEDS; discontinuous 13.86), so the dataset, while valuable, exposes unresolved modeling challenges rather than demonstrating solved ones; rare categories (reverse-order at 1.01%, Reason argument type at 0.05%) are so sparse that subset evaluations may be unstable.

Baseline comparability is somewhat complicated: discriminative models are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, and EAE-only baselines all condition on Tagprime triggers, so differences across model families conflate capability with evaluation-scope choices.

The paper claims 'larger scale' but RAMS has ~5x more tokens and 139 event types; scale advantage holds mainly in events/documents ratio, and the abstract-only scope limits coverage compared to document-level datasets like DocEE.

strengths: The paper presents a complete and carefully documented contribution: a large-scale document-level scientific EE dataset (SciEvents, 2,508 abstracts / 24,381 events / 56,411 arguments) with a multi-stage annotation pipeline, a formal protocol for supervisors/annotators, fair remuneration reporting, and released resources, which supports reproducibility.

The benchmarking effort is substantial and fairly conducted: a broad set of baselines spanning global, discriminative, and generative paradigms (adapted via TextEE or official code), three runs per model with variance reported, shared backbones, and adapted evaluation protocols for EAE-only and generative models.

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: subset evaluations on complex nugget/event forms (discontinuous, overlapping, reverse-order, sub-event), identification and classification error analyses, and new complexity/density statistics that position SciEvents against prior domain datasets (Tables 2 and 4).

The grid-based formulation (HTL/THL/EAL relations) is coherently motivated and technically well specified: loss, inference, decoding algorithm, complexity analysis, hyperparameters, and training costs are all provided.

The paper is honest about its shortcomings, e.g., acknowledging that discontinuous/overlapping/reverse-order extraction remains weak and that AC performance is modest, and includes a clear limitations section on abstract-level and NLP-only domain scope.
weaknesses: No inter-annotator agreement (IAA/kappa) is reported for the dataset. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a substitute; for a dataset paper whose central claims rest on annotation quality, this is a significant soundness gap.

The claimed complexity advantage of SciEvents over other datasets (Table 2) is only partially verifiable: the #D/#R/#S columns are '–' for all baselines because those structures were never annotated, so the claim that scientific text is structurally more complex is established only relative to datasets that could not express such structures.

The headline methodological contribution has limited novelty: word-word grid/relational modeling of entities, relations, and events is well established (e.g., REGRID, UIE, unified semantic matching), and the gains over the strongest baselines are small (e.g., +0.51 AC, +0.53 EC), in places comparable to the reported standard deviations.

The grid method is only evaluated on SciEvents, which the authors themselves build and tailor; the framework's claimed general effectiveness for complex event structures is not validated on external benchmarks with complex forms (e.g., Genia sub-events), limiting the strength of the SOTA claim.

Dataset scope is narrow: ACL main-conference NLP abstracts only (single sub-domain, abstracts only), which the limitations section concedes limits generalizability; the random 80/10/10 split of documents from the same source and period also raises questions about evaluation of generalization.

Several design decisions lack justification or ablation: the need for the BiLSTM + CLN on top of RoBERTa is asserted rather than analyzed; the EC metric conflates trigger-as-argument events with general hierarchical relations; per-type argument constraints in the schema make decoding dependent on ontology checks whose sensitivity is not examined.

Writing is generally clear but some comparisons are overclaimed relative to evidence (e.g., describing ~0.5-point margins as a notable advantage), and the dataset-density narrative partially conflates rhetorical structure of abstracts with domain properties.
